Multi-modality yields valuable complementary information for medical prediction, yet missing data within clinical cohorts frequently prevents the use these approaches. Consequently, existing imputation struggles when data is missing across heterogeneous sources (e.g., image versus textual) or when a single modacity suffers extensive dropout, limiting multi-learning capabilities. To solve this challenge, our proposed method models a Conditional Bidirectional Generative Adversarial Network known as the Conditional Probabilistically-Bidisciplinary Imputative GNet (C-PBIGNet) which utilizes partial bidisciplinary GNet (PBGI). The new C-PBIGNet incorporates a joint condition latent representation that aligns available multi-modality inputs and utilizes discriminative information, alongside class-conditional GNet (C-PBIGNet). It is now only possible to infer the distribution of image/non-text/structured data for conditional learning, addressing imputeability challenges within heterogeneous environments. Using two datasets from National Cancer Trial Institute's NLCT and external validation groups, the C-PBIGNet generated significantly fewer prediction error rates, particularly regarding its predictive AUC (Acc: +5%), outperform current methods including conditional-pBIGNet and PBGN. Thus our analysis demonstrates the model for accurate imaging/non-text/structured prediction capabilities.

Recent studies highlight the successful application of neural style transfer, but most methods limit stylization to the pixel domain, an approach deemed imperfect as real paintings are composed of brushstrokes rather than pixels. This work argues for moving to brushstroke-level stylization within an existing image-based style transfer framework to better capture stylistic intent. This research introduces a differentiable technique to generate images parameterized instead of pixels. This approach delivers substantially higher visual quality and affords greater stylistic flexibility than its predecessors, enabling enhanced interaction. Comprehensive evaluations further demonstrate the benefits of utilizing a generative, parameter-based image stylization method in image-based style transfer models.
